results.reason: Every condition is met on the printed figures. The reader's open point, condition 3, does not fail on the rule's text. (1) Same question: MCI-to-AD conversion in ADNI MCI. P-203 uses T1 MRI. P-212 is multimodal, and its MRI input (FreeSurfer total hippocampal volume) is the feature its own impurity analysis ranks first, so the MRI channel is shared as the rule's multimodal clause requires. Horizon, predictor set, ADNI phases and validation design are allowed differences. (6) The record's 91.1% is P-203's AD vs CN figure, so the pair is judged on the printed conversion accuracy of 0.801. The gap does not come from that misreading. (2) Accuracy against accuracy. (4) P-203's 0.801 has a Wilson interval of [0.753, 0.841]. P-212's test accuracies are 0.683 [0.602, 0.755] (ensemble) and 0.662 [0.580, 0.735] (random forest). Each estimate lies outside the other's interval. This also holds on the 0.775 that P-203's own sensitivity and specificity imply ([0.726, 0.818] excludes 0.683, and 0.775 exceeds 0.755). (5) No figure reaches 0.97. (3) Neither paper reports a result under the other's condition. P-203 reports no conversion result at a near-balanced class mix: it declined the ADNI-2 -> ADNI-1 conversion experiment 'because of the lack of sufficient pMCI samples in ADNI-2'. It also reports no cognitive or hippocampal-volume input and no unbounded horizon. P-212 reports no whole-image model, no 36-month window and no ADNI-2-only test. Suppose the per-class figures are counted as same-subset figures. They still do not agree. Sensitivities agree (0.520 [0.409, 0.629] vs 0.615-0.631), but specificities exclude each other in both directions: 0.856 [0.805, 0.894] vs 0.703 [0.591, 0.795] and 0.730 [0.619, 0.818]. The rule drops a pair only when the matched figures agree within uncertainty. Here one subset disagrees, so the gap moves into that subset rather than dissolving. The balanced accuracies, and the reweighting of P-203's per-class figures to P-212's 47% converter mix (0.699), are the reader's derivations; neither paper prints them. The reweighting is also indeterminate, because P-203's figures are internally inconsistent. P-203 prints SEN 0.520 next to ACC 0.801 twice (Table 4, and the SAM ablation on p.10: 'the ACC and SEN is 0.772 vs. 0.801 and 0.440 vs. 0.520'). If both are right, specificity must be 214/241 = 0.888, and the reweighted figure is 0.716. If the printed 0.856 is right, sensitivity must be 47/75 = 0.627, and the reweighted figure is 0.749, which lies outside P-212's random-forest interval. Class mix and operating threshold are therefore the leading candidate explanation, and a strong one, but neither paper shows it is sufficient. If the operator judges that the class-mix arithmetic alone dissolves the headline gap, the pair fails condition 3 on that judgment, not on any matched figure either paper prints.

The printed figures cannot all be true: ACC 0.801 with SEN 0.520 implies SPE 214/241 = 0.888; with SPE 0.856 it implies SEN 47/75 = 0.627. Majority-class rate 241/316 = 0.763, inside P-203's own accuracy interval. AUC Hanley-McNeil (75/241): SE 0.0332, [0.724, 0.854].

Stable subset: 0.856 [0.805, 0.894] vs 0.703 [0.591, 0.795] and 0.730 [0.619, 0.818], which exclude each other in both directions, so they disagree.

candidate_explanations: Class mix of the evaluation sets: 24% converters in P-203's ADNI-2 test vs 47% in P-212's test. P-203 quote: 'The ADNI-2 dataset has 643 3T T1W sMR brain images, including 143 AD, 184 CN, 75 pMCI, and 241 sMCI.' P-212 quote: 'converters to AD (cAD; n = 321, 47.3%)'. P-203's 0.801 lies close to its majority-class rate (0.763). This is the leading explanation; neither paper shows it is sufficient.

Operating threshold: P-203 favours specificity (SPE 0.856 at SEN 0.520), P-212 is near-symmetric (SPE 0.730, SEN 0.631). P-203's threshold was learned on ADNI-1 at 42% converters and applied to ADNI-2 at 24%.

Label definition and horizon. P-203: 'Progressive MCI (pMCI): Subjects are diagnosed with MCI who would gradually progress to AD within 0-36 months'; stable over 0-90 months. P-212: converters at any later visit vs stable at all visits, with at least 3 visits.

Predictor set: whole-brain T1 through a multiview-slice attention plus 3D CNN (P-203) vs neuropsychological tests, one hippocampal volume, APOE and demographics in RF/ensemble (P-212). P-212 quote: 'with cognitive function, hippocampal volume and genetic APOE status as features, we obtained a cross-validation classification accuracy of about 70%.' The difference would lead one to expect P-212 to score higher, not lower.

Validation design: cross-phase, cross-field-strength test in P-203 (trained ADNI-1 1.5 T, tested ADNI-2 3 T) vs a stratified internal 79/21 split in P-212, whose test accuracy (66-68%) falls below its own CV mean (about 75%). P-212 quote: 'When the model was evaluated on our unseen test set, the overall classification accuracy was 66.2%.'

Reporting inconsistency in P-203: its printed ACC 0.801 does not match its own SEN/SPE on the stated test set (0.775). P-203 quote (Table 4, p.6): 'MSA3D 0.911 0.888 0.914 0.950 0.898 0.801 0.520 0.856 0.789 0.553'.

results.reason: The reader's only open point is condition 1, and P-41's own pages settle it in favour of a shared clinical question. P-41's title is 'Early progression detection from MCI to AD using multi-view MRI', and its framework is built 'to predict the progression of MCI to pMCI/AD' (p.6). On p.3 it cites Luo et al. [29] as prior work on its own problem: 'a novel attention transfer method that trains a 3D CNN to predict the likelihood of MCI progressing to AD within three years', first trained on a source task and then 'to simultaneously classify sMCI and pMCI'. That wording matches P-3's abstract (Luo et al., 'Class activation attention transfer neural networks for MCI conversion prediction'). The extracted text does not include P-41's reference list, so the identification rests on that match. P-41's Table 5 also sets its 91.77% beside other sMCI-vs-pMCI accuracies (77.2%, 73.54%, 75.2%), so P-41 itself treats its figure as a result for this question. Its positive class is 81 converters plus 15 AD patients: 84% are pMCI, and all are ADNI Alzheimer's-spectrum participants. That is a label-definition difference, which the rule lists among candidate explanations. It is not the kind of population-class difference the rule excludes, such as Parkinson's patients against Alzheimer's-spectrum MCI. The admixture is not shown to explain the gap. P-41 does not say how the 15 AD patients were split across train, validation and test. Suppose they fell in the test positives in the same proportion (15.6%) and were perfectly separated. The converter-only AUC would then be (0.9287 - 0.156)/0.844 = 0.915, still above P-3's upper bound of 0.817. The admixture alone would close the gap only if at least 61% of the 15 test positives, 9 or 10 patients, were perfectly ranked AD cases. Conditions 2-6 hold. Both papers report accuracy and ROC-AUC. Neither reports a matched figure: P-41 has no AD-excluded, whole-volume or 36-month result, and P-3 has no result with AD in the positive class. AUC 0.9287 [0.830, 1.000] against 0.780 [0.743, 0.817] excludes in both directions (z = 0.149/sqrt(0.019^2 + 0.0505^2) = 2.76). Accuracy 0.9177 [0.766, 0.974] against 0.7461 [0.710, 0.779] also excludes in both directions. On the 0.881 that P-41's own sensitivity and specificity imply on a balanced 15/15 test ([0.720, 0.955]), P-41's estimate still lies outside P-3's interval, and one direction is enough. P-41's figures are below 0.97, so the Section 3.5 exclusion does not apply despite the 30-subject internal test. The record's figures are printed as recorded; it omits the AD admixture, which is listed here as an explanation. None of the candidate explanations is shown to be sufficient.

Wilson n = 30: [0.766, 0.974]. On a balanced 15/15 test, accuracy must equal the SEN/SPE mean, 0.881, Wilson [0.720, 0.955]. Hanley-McNeil 15/15: Q1 = 0.8669, Q2 = 0.8944, SE 0.0505, [0.830, 1.000].
figures.admixture_bound: Positive class 81 pMCI + 15 AD = 96 (15.6% AD). If test positives hold AD in the same share and AD is ranked perfectly, the converter-only AUC is (0.9287 - 0.156)/0.844 = 0.915 > 0.817. AD share needed to bring the converter-only AUC to 0.817: (0.9287 - 0.817)/(1 - 0.817) = 0.61 of test positives.

candidate_explanations: Label definition: AD patients in P-41's positive class. P-41 quote (p.8): 'Furthermore, we added 15 patients with AD to the pMCI group to help the model learn both the progressive and fully diseased brain patterns simultaneously.' Not shown to be sufficient (see admixture_bound).

Label windows: M18-M48 converters against stability to M48 (P-41) vs dementia within 36 months against staying MCI (P-3). P-41 quote: 'The second group (pMCI) included 81 participants who were diagnosed with MCI at baseline but progressed to AD within 2.5 years, between month 18 (M18) and M48.'

Evaluation-set size and model selection: a 30-subject test set on which P-41 compares many ensemble and head configurations, vs 5-fold CV over 593. P-41 quote: 'all results reported in this study were based on the test set.'

Input representation and architecture: 132 middle slices per plane through a heterogeneous 2D CNN ensemble with CBAM and multi-head attention (P-41) vs whole 3D volumes through a 3D CNN with transferred attention maps (P-3). P-41 quote: 'From each volume, 132 middle slices from the axial, coronal, and sagittal planes were selected'.

Cohort and scanner: 192 ADNI-1/GO/2 3 T subjects selected on data availability (P-41) vs 593 ADNI-1/2 subjects on the Wen et al. benchmark splits (P-3). P-3 quote: 'We performed 5 fold cross validation using the same data splits as that used in [11]'.
Reporting inconsistency in P-41: its printed accuracy (91.77%) exceeds both its sensitivity (87.69%) and its specificity (88.53%), which a balanced 15/15 test cannot produce.

Evaluation bias acknowledged by P-3, which would inflate P-3 rather than P-41. P-3 quote: 'the use of 5 fold cross validation for both tuning and selecting the models. This may lead to an optimistically biased evaluation of the model performance.'

results.reason: Condition 1 fails. As recorded, the pair sets P-1153's ADNI MCI-to-AD iAUC (0.787) against P-1154's direct CN-to-AD AUC (0.994), which are different baseline populations and endpoints. The strongest case is the NC-to-MCI question both papers print, with FDG-PET as the shared channel. There, conditions 2-6 are met. P-1153's HABS Model 1 (clinical features + FDG SUVR, the closest analogue of P-1154's FDG z-score plus baseline cognition) gives iAUC 0.817 (0.692-0.909). P-1154's MCI-as-first-event AUCs are 0.686, 0.643 and 0.680, with a CV mean of 0.670; each lies outside P-1153's interval, although 0.686 misses by only 0.006. P-1153's 0.817 lies outside P-1154's Hanley-McNeil interval [0.655, 0.717], and would still lie outside [0.616, 0.756] if only a 20% temporal split was scored. No matched figure exists: P-1153 prints no fixed-horizon HABS AUC and P-1154 prints no iAUC. Two of the reader's three reasons for doubting P-1154's CN label do not hold. First, the direct-conversion group's 'MMSE: 21.0' is the cognitive-reserve index, which Table 1's notes define as 'MMSE - (ADAS/3)'; the stable group's 26.9 is the same index. So it does not contradict the MMSE >= 24 criterion. Second, Table 4's event counts barely move from 12 to 36 months (514/520/525), while Table 2 gives a median time to any decline of 2.9-6.2 years, so those counts are not 12-month incidences. They do not show 45% reaching MCI within a year. The third reason stands on P-1154's own pages. Table 3 stratifies 'Baseline Cognitive Status' into 'MMSE 20-23 (Mild Impairment)' and 'ADAS >=30 (Severe Impairment)', and the text refers to 'participants with MCI at baseline (MMSE 20-23)'. Both contradict its definition of CN (MMSE >= 24, CDR 0), for strata whose size is not reported. With 67% of P-1154's cohort progressing and 16.5% going directly to dementia, against 8% progressing in HABS, the population behind P-1154's CN label cannot be established as the cognitively normal older adults of HABS. If the operator takes P-1154's stated inclusion criteria as defining its population, and treats those strata as reporting defects, every other condition is met and the pair would qualify with the explanations listed, none shown to be sufficient.

figures.cn_label_check: The reader's 'MMSE 21.0' is P-1154's cognitive-reserve index (Table 1 notes: 'Cognitive reserve calculated as MMSE - (ADAS/3)'), so that reason is a misreading. The Table 4 events (514/520/525) do not fit 12-month incidence given Table 2's median time to decline of 2.9-6.2 y, so that reason is not established. Still standing: Table 3 'MMSE 20-23 (Mild Impairment)' and 'ADAS >=30 (Severe Impairment)' baseline strata, and the text 'participants with MCI at baseline (MMSE 20-23)', against the stated CN criteria MMSE >= 24, CDR 0.

candidate_explanations: Applicable only if condition 1 is accepted. Population behind the label: P-1154's CN cohort includes baseline strata it calls MCI (MMSE 20-23) and severe impairment (ADAS >= 30), and its progression base rate is far above HABS's (67% vs 8%). P-1154 quote (p.5): 'Among participants with MCI at baseline (MMSE 20-23), low FDG metabolism resulted in six-fold higher risk'.

Metric construction: Cox-model iAUC integrated over follow-up and fitted within HABS (P-1153) vs fixed-horizon ROC AUC from a cross-validated multinomial pathway model (P-1154). P-1153 quote: 'calculating the integrated area under the time-dependent ROC curves (iAUC) for Cox regression models'.
Predictors: age, gender, education, APOE4, PACC and FDG SUVR (P-1153) vs FDG MetaROI z-score 'supplemented by baseline cognitive measures when appropriate' (P-1154).

Event count: 22 HABS progressors, which P-1153 itself calls 'a relatively small number of progressors to MCI' giving 'less robust validation for NC subjects', vs more than 500 MCI-first events in P-1154.
Validation: in-cohort Cox fit in HABS with resampling only for the model comparison (P-1153) vs temporal and subject-grouped cross-validation within ADNI (P-1154).

results.reason: I found no printed figure that makes this pair qualify. Condition 4 fails, and condition 1 fails as well. The only shared outcome on a shared metric is executive function as an SMD. P-833's pooled SMD of -0.19 (-0.74 to 0.36) contains P-834's TMT-A -0.24, TMT-B -0.28 and Stroop reaction-time -0.31. P-833's -0.19 lies inside all three P-834 intervals. The intervals overlap, neither estimate excludes the other, and the difference is one of statistical significance only: 4 trials (188 participants across the whole review) against pools of 280 to 1,104. I also checked P-833's sensitivity analyses (Table 3), its only other EF figures. Omitting Amjad gives +0.07 (-0.36 to 0.50). That estimate lies outside P-834's TMT intervals, but P-834's estimates lie inside its interval and the intervals overlap from -0.36 to -0.12. A significant estimate against a non-significant one without mutual exclusion does not qualify. The other omissions (-0.30, -0.34, -0.22) fall inside P-834's TMT-A interval. Reversing P-833's sign convention does not help either: the aligned interval (-0.36 to 0.74) still contains all three P-834 estimates. No other shared outcome has the same metric. P-833's memory result is an SMD (-0.03, -0.60 to 0.55, 47 participants), while P-834's memory-type pools are single-instrument MDs (DR 0.61, VLT 1.06), and P-834 pools no global cognition to set against P-833's MD of 2.66. The record's own contrast (DR MD 0.61 against global-cognition MD 2.66) compares different outcomes and scales, which is a condition-6 misreading. Condition 1 also fails. P-834 excludes 'exercise training combined with other non-exercise activities such as cognitive training, drugs supplementation, or virtual games', which is exactly P-833's intervention. P-833's controls include cognitive-only, physical-only and combined training, so its contrast is partly VR-combined training against exercise. The operator named this pair. On the sources it is a gap in significance between different interventions, not a discrepancy in effect.
